2: And every Jew needs to cherish Eretz Yisrael and come to it from the ends of the earth with great longing—like a child [running] to their mother’s embrace. For the root of our sin, which caused crying for generations, was that we despised it, as it says: “They rejected the desirable land” (Psalms 106:24). But in the redemption of our souls, may it soon, it is written: “For Thy servants hold her stones dear, and cherish her very dust” (Psalms 102:15), and there it says: “Thou wilt arise, and have mercy upon Zion” (Psalms 102:14). And therefore, the Amoraim would kiss its dust and its stones when they arrived there. And how good and how pleasant it is to sing a song of affection composed about it by Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi with great love—the beginning of the poem: “O holy land, precious and beloved,” etc. So too we sing by the memorial of Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai every Rosh Chodesh eve with great joy, and we plead with God that He not send us out from upon it. Also those near and those far who are outside it should yearn and long for it, for just as God chose them, so too He chose Eretz Yisrael and designated it for them. And they are not called “one nation” except with it, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explained the verse: “And who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land” (I Samuel 7:23).

And we find in the Midrash that the Holy One, blessed be He, first told Avraham Avinu to go to Eretz Yisrael, and see it, and return. And after he returned, he was not permitted to go back for five years—and during those five years he longed intensely to go to return. And [about this] he said this verse: “Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then I would fly away, and be at rest. Lo, then I would wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Sela.” (Psalms 55:7–8)—better to dwell in the deserts of Eretz Yisrael than in the palaces of the Diaspora.And he was longing, and when he was permitted [to go] it is written “So Avram departed, as Hashem had spoken to him” (Genesis 12:4). Before he came to the land, he did not yet long for it—but after he came once and saw, through prophetic vision, the precious beauty of its holiness, he yearned for it deeply. From him we learn for all generations—we, his descendants—that we too should long as he did, even though its inhabitants suffer; for that reason, we should accept suffering with joy.

This explains why the section about Amalek is juxtaposed with entering Eretz Yisrael in Parashas Ki Tavo. As the Sages, peace be upon them, said: The Holy one, blessed be he, gave Israel three gifts, and all were given through suffering: the Torah, Eretz Yisrael, and the World to Come. Just as Amalek came during the first entry [into the land], so too at the ingathering of exiles—when Jews seek to come to Eretz Yisrael—Amalek arises against them on the way, as we see even today. May Hashem see and judge.

The section begins with the word “והיה” (“and it shall be”), which is one of the twelve combinations of the Holy Name—hinting that one who dwells in Eretz Yisrael is attached to Hashem; the opposite of one who dwells outside the land—like a Jew who is considered as if he has no God. This wording also alludes to what they, peace be upon them, said: every place where “והיה” appears, it denotes joy.

And the Ramban writes, in counting [the] 613 [commandments], that dwelling in the Eretz Yisrael is a mitzvah fulfilled at every moment one is there. And it is known that the main reward of a mitzvah comes from the great joy with which it is performed, as it says: “Because you did not serve Hashem your God with joy…” (Deuteronomy 28:47). If so, one who lives in Eretz Yisrael must be constantly joyful in this constant mitzvah, out of love for it—and also must be fearful and reverent, as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wrote: any commandment not performed with love and awe is not truly a commandment. Therefore they said in Avos D’Rabbi Nasan: “Be joyful and trembling regarding the commandments.” And behold, the word “והיה” by the Mitzvah of settling Eretz Yisrael hints to the joy of the mitzvah, and the juxtaposition of the paragraph to Amalek hints to the trembling in the Mitzvah from the strip which is hung in the sky. And the afflictions of Eretz Yisrael—whether from nations or from illness—serve as an altar of atonement, as it says: “No inhabitant shall say ‘I am sick’; the people who dwell there are forgiven their iniquity” (Isaiah 33:24).

This is also hinted in the verse “And it shall be, when thou art come in to the land which the Lord thy God gives thee for an inheritance” (Deuteronomy 26:1), whose final letters form נכ״ה—as in “He deducts (menaceh) for him from the money”(Bava Metziah 105b), like Rashi writes on the verse “perhaps I shall prevail, that we may smite (naceh)  them” (Numbers 22:6), meaning that through the hardships in Eretz Yisrael, sins are diminished and reduced, and the nation that dwells in it is free of iniquity. And it says: “and He will atone for His land [and] His people” (Deuteronomy 32:43). This applies particularly to lighter sins, when one repents and regrets them—these sufferings cleanse them, and at death, a person proceeds straight to Gan Eden.
